title: Regulating and cross-drainage structures
summary: The cross-drainage works are distinguished by one question only — which one passes over the other. Canal over drain is an aqueduct, drain over canal a super-passage, and the siphon versions are those in which the lower one flows under pressure. For outlets, the concept to understand is flexibility: a proportional outlet with flexibility of one distributes a shortage fairly among all farmers, which is why it is preferred in a water-scarce system. Escapes exist to protect the canal from breaching, not to dispose of surplus water conveniently.

sections.heading: Cross-drainage works
sections.body:
**Why they exist.** A **contour canal** must cross every natural drainage coming down the slope. Since both the canal and the drain must continue, one must pass over the other — and the choice of which, and how, defines the type of work.

**The classification is decided by ONE question: which passes over the other?**

| Work | Canal | Drain | Drain flows |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aqueduct** | **OVER** (in a trough or flume) | Under | **Freely, at atmospheric pressure** |
| **Siphon aqueduct** | **OVER** | Under | **UNDER PRESSURE** (siphonic) |
| **Super-passage** | Under | **OVER** | Freely |
| **Canal siphon (siphon)** | **Under, UNDER PRESSURE** | Over | Freely |
| **Level crossing** | Both at the **same level**, the flows mixing and being separated by regulators | — | — |
| **Inlet and outlet** | The drain is **admitted into** the canal and taken out further along | — | — |

**The mnemonic that settles most questions:** the name describes what the **CANAL** does. An **aqueduct carries the canal over**; a **super-passage lets the drain pass above**; a **canal siphon takes the canal under, siphonically**.

**The "siphon" qualifier always means the LOWER channel flows under pressure**, because its bed has had to be depressed below its natural level to squeeze under the upper one. So:

> **Aqueduct** — canal over, drain flows **freely** beneath
> **Siphon aqueduct** — canal over, **drain forced under pressure** beneath
> **Super-passage** — drain over, canal flows freely beneath
> **Canal siphon** — drain over, **canal forced under pressure** beneath

**How the type is chosen — by relative bed and water levels:**

| Level relation | Work |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed comfortably ABOVE the drain's HFL** | **Aqueduct** — the natural and preferred choice |
| Canal bed above the drain bed but **not above its HFL** | **Siphon aqueduct** — the drain must be depressed and run under pressure |
| **Drain bed ABOVE the canal's FSL** | **Super-passage** |
| Drain bed above the canal bed but not above its FSL | **Canal siphon** |
| Levels **nearly equal**, and both discharges large | **Level crossing** (a last resort) |
| A **small** drain, and its water is acceptable in the canal | **Inlet–outlet** |

**The aqueduct is preferred wherever the levels permit**, for several reasons: the **canal water stays clean** (no drain water enters it), the drain flows **freely** without the head loss and silting risk of a pressure barrel, the canal's flow is **uninterrupted**, and maintenance of both is straightforward.

**A level crossing is a last resort**, and the reason is worth stating: it **mixes the silty drain water into the canal**, degrading the canal water and depositing silt in it, and it requires **two regulators** (one on the canal, one on the drain) to be operated in coordination during every flood. It is used only where the levels leave no alternative and both discharges are too large for a structure.

**Design considerations for a siphon aqueduct** — the most demanding of the types:

| Consideration | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Barrel velocity** | **2 to 3 m/s** — high enough to be **self-cleansing** (the barrel cannot be scoured by gravity), low enough to limit head loss |
| **Head loss** through the barrel | Computed from entry, friction and exit losses; determines the **afflux** upstream of the drain |
| **Uplift on the barrel roof** | The **canal trough above** presses down, but when the canal is **empty** the drain's pressure can **lift the roof** — so the empty-canal case must be checked |
| **Uplift on the floor** | Seepage from the canal above can lift the barrel floor |
| **Scour** upstream and downstream | Protection by aprons and cut-offs |
| **Transitions** | Contraction and expansion of the canal into and out of the flume, to limit losses |

**The empty-canal uplift case is the design trap.** The barrel is designed to carry the weight of the canal and its water — but when the canal is closed for maintenance while the drain is in flood, the load reverses and the barrel roof is in **uplift**. A barrel designed only for the loaded case fails then, and the failure occurs at the least expected moment.

**Transitions.** Where the canal is flumed (narrowed) to cross, the change of section must be **gradual** to limit the energy loss and avoid disturbance. Typical contractions of **2:1** and expansions of **3:1** to **4:1** are used — the expansion always **flatter than the contraction**, because a decelerating flow separates far more readily than an accelerating one. That asymmetry is a general principle in hydraulic transitions and is worth remembering.

**Fluming** the canal through the structure is done to reduce the length and cost of the trough, but it raises the velocity and hence the head loss, so there is an economic optimum. The canal is usually **lined through the flumed length** to permit the higher velocity.

sections.heading: Canal regulation works
sections.body:
**Regulators control the flow; escapes dispose of it.**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Canal head regulator** | Controls the discharge **admitted from the river** into the canal; excludes silt and floods |
| **Distributary head regulator** | Controls the discharge into an **offtaking** channel |
| **Cross regulator** | Placed **in the parent canal, DOWNSTREAM of an offtake**; **raises the upstream water level** so the offtake can draw its full supply |
| **Canal escape** | **Discharges surplus water OUT of the canal** |
| **Canal fall** | Drops the bed level where the ground is steeper than the canal |
| **Canal outlet (module)** | Delivers water from a distributary to a **watercourse** |
| Metering flume | Measures the discharge |

**The cross regulator and distributary head regulator are almost always built as a PAIR**, and the reason explains what a cross regulator is for. When the parent canal runs at less than full supply, its water level falls, and the offtake — whose sill is set for full supply level — can no longer draw its share. A **cross regulator downstream of the offtake** is partly closed, which **pens up the water upstream** and restores the level at the offtake sill. So:

> **The cross regulator's purpose is to RAISE the upstream level, not to control the downstream flow** — though it does both.

Its secondary functions: it allows the canal to be **closed downstream** for maintenance while the upper reach continues to supply, it helps **regulate the water surface** through the system, and it often carries a **road bridge**.

**Canal escapes** — and their purpose is protective, not convenient:

> An escape exists to **protect the canal from BREACHING**.

The situations requiring one:

| Situation | Why the escape is needed |
|---|---|
| **A downstream outlet or regulator is closed** suddenly | The water backs up and would **overtop and breach** the bank |
| **Rain makes irrigation unnecessary** | The supply already in the canal must go somewhere |
| **A breach or emergency downstream** | The canal must be emptied quickly |
| **Silt has accumulated** | A scouring escape flushes it out |
| The canal must be **emptied for maintenance** | — |

**Types:**

| Escape | Character |
|---|---|
| **Tail escape** | At the **end** of the canal; maintains a minimum flow and prevents stagnation at the tail |
| **Surplus water escape** | At intervals along the canal, to discharge excess |
| **Scouring escape** | With its **sill at or near the canal bed**, so it can **flush silt** as well as water |

The escape discharges into a **natural drainage, a river, or a depression**, and its capacity is usually taken as about **half the canal's full supply discharge** — enough to lower the level quickly without an excessively large structure.

**A canal without adequate escapes is a canal that will breach**, and a breach in a canal running in high embankment is a serious matter: it floods and erodes the land below, cuts the supply to everything downstream, and takes weeks to repair. That is why escapes are provided at intervals and at every point where a downstream closure could pen up water.

**Trash rack.** At the head of a canal, hydropower intake or pipeline, a **trash rack** prevents **floating debris and large objects** entering the waterway. Its design points:

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Bar spacing** | Set by the smallest passage downstream — a turbine runner, a pump, a pipe |
| **Approach velocity** | Kept **low (about 1 m/s or less)** so debris does not pin itself against the bars |
| **Inclination** | Sloped, so debris can be **raked upward** |
| Head loss | Rises sharply as it clogs — hence raking is a **routine operating task** |
| Access | A working platform for raking; mechanical rakes on large installations |

The **low approach velocity** requirement is the one candidates overlook. A high approach velocity presses debris firmly against the rack, where it accumulates, blocks progressively, and eventually starves the intake — and the head loss then rises just when the discharge is most needed.

sections.heading: Canal outlets and flexibility
sections.body:
A **canal outlet (module)** is the small structure delivering water from a **distributary** to a farmer's **watercourse**. It is the point at which the public system meets the private, so it must be **equitable, tamper-resistant and simple**.

**Requirements of a good outlet:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Cheap and simple** | Thousands are needed in a system |
| **Tamper-proof** | Farmers have every incentive to enlarge their own |
| **Free of moving parts** | Nothing to break or be stolen |
| **Not liable to silt up or be blocked** | It must work unattended |
| **Draw its fair share of silt** | An outlet drawing clear water leaves the silt to deposit in the distributary |
| **Predictable discharge** | For equitable distribution and for design |
| Minimum head loss | Preserves command downstream |

**The fifth requirement is the least obvious and worth explaining.** If an outlet draws only the **clear upper layer** of water, the **silt remains in the distributary** and deposits there, progressively silting the channel and requiring costly clearance. So a well-designed outlet must **draw water in proportion to the silt it should take** — which means drawing from a depth that gives it a representative sediment concentration.

**Classification of outlets:**

| Type | Discharge depends on | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-modular (rigid)** | **BOTH** the distributary level **and** the watercourse level | Simplest — a pipe or open cut. Discharge varies with both, so it is unpredictable |
| **Semi-modular (flexible)** | **ONLY the distributary level** | Independent of the watercourse level; the commonest practical type |
| **Modular (rigid module)** | **NEITHER** — delivers a **CONSTANT discharge** | Independent of both levels within a working range |

**Examples:**

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Non-modular | Submerged pipe outlet, masonry sluice |
| **Semi-modular** | **Kennedy's gauge outlet**, **open flume outlet**, **orifice semi-module (adjustable proportional module, APM)** |
| **Modular** | **Gibb's module** |

**Flexibility** is the quantitative measure of an outlet's behaviour:

> **Flexibility F = (dq/q) / (dQ/Q)**

that is, the **ratio of the proportionate change in the outlet's discharge to the proportionate change in the distributary's discharge**.

| Flexibility | Name | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **F = 1** | **PROPORTIONAL** | The outlet's discharge changes **in the same proportion** as the parent channel's |
| **F > 1** | **Hyper-proportional** | The outlet takes a **disproportionately large** share when supply falls short |
| **F < 1** | **Sub-proportional** | The outlet takes a **disproportionately small** share when supply falls short |

**Why proportionality (F = 1) is the desirable property**, and this is the substance of the topic:

> When the distributary runs short — as it does whenever the river or the main canal cannot supply the full demand — a **proportional** outlet **shares the shortage equally** among all farmers, each receiving the same **percentage** of their entitlement.

An outlet with **F > 1** takes more than its share in a shortage, so farmers on such outlets are advantaged and others suffer disproportionately; one with **F < 1** suffers unfairly. In a water-scarce system, where shortage is normal rather than exceptional, **equity in shortage is the central requirement of distribution**, and proportionality delivers it automatically without any operator intervention.

That is why the **proportional outlet is the design objective**, and why **Setting** and **Sensitivity** are the related quantities:

> **Setting = the height of the outlet crest above the distributary bed ÷ the depth of water in the distributary**

For an outlet to be proportional, its setting must satisfy a particular relation to the type of outlet — **proportionality is achieved by choice of setting**, not by chance.

> **Sensitivity = (dq/q) / (dG/D)**, the rate of change of outlet discharge with the change in the parent channel's water **level**

A **modular** outlet has **zero sensitivity** (its discharge does not respond to level at all), which is ideal for guaranteed delivery but means it cannot share a shortage — it either delivers its full discharge or, once the level falls below its working range, nothing.

**Gibb's module** achieves constant discharge by an ingenious arrangement: water enters a **rising spiral channel** in which it is made to spin, and a series of **baffles** dissipates exactly the surplus head, so that the discharge is independent of the upstream head over a range. It has no moving parts, which satisfies the tamper-proof requirement — but it is expensive and liable to silt, which is why semi-modules dominate in practice.

**Warabandi and the outlet.** The outlet is where the **rotational water supply (warabandi)** system operates: the outlet delivers a fixed discharge to the watercourse, and the **farmers within that watercourse take turns** to receive the whole of it for a fixed time on a published roster. The engineering and the institution are therefore designed together — the outlet fixes the discharge, and the roster allocates the time.

**The logic of warabandi is worth stating**, because it is not obvious why giving each farmer the whole flow briefly is better than giving each a share continuously:

| Continuous small share | Rotational whole flow |
|---|---|
| Flow too small to irrigate **efficiently** | **Large enough** to advance across a field quickly, with less percolation loss |
| **Hard to measure or verify** — theft is easy and invisible | **Verifiable** — a farmer taking water out of turn is obvious |
| Distribution structures must divide flow precisely | Only the **timing** must be managed |
| No incentive to economise | The turn is finite, so water is used carefully |

So warabandi converts a **difficult hydraulic problem** (dividing a small flow accurately among many users) into a **simple institutional one** (keeping to a roster) — which is why it has persisted for over a century and why Nepal's farmer-managed systems arrived independently at similar arrangements.

formulas.label: Cross-drainage classification
formulas.expression: Aqueduct: canal OVER, drain free. Siphon aqueduct: canal over, drain UNDER PRESSURE. Super-passage: drain over, canal free. Canal siphon: canal UNDER PRESSURE, drain over.
formulas.note: The name describes what the CANAL does. "Siphon" always means the lower channel flows under pressure.

formulas.label: Selecting the cross-drainage type
formulas.expression: Canal bed above drain HFL → aqueduct. Drain bed above canal FSL → super-passage. Levels close → siphon versions or level crossing.
formulas.note: The aqueduct is preferred wherever levels permit — canal water stays clean and the drain flows freely.

formulas.label: Siphon barrel velocity
formulas.note: Self-cleansing (the barrel cannot be scoured by gravity) but limiting head loss. Check the EMPTY-canal uplift case.

formulas.label: Transition ratios
formulas.note: The expansion is always flatter, because decelerating flow separates far more readily than accelerating flow.

formulas.label: Outlet flexibility
formulas.note: F = 1 shares a shortage EQUALLY among all farmers — the central requirement in a water-scarce system.

formulas.label: Outlet setting and sensitivity
formulas.expression: Setting = crest height above bed / depth of water ;   Sensitivity = (dq/q)/(dG/D)
formulas.note: Proportionality is achieved by CHOICE OF SETTING. A modular outlet has zero sensitivity.

formulas.label: Outlet classification
formulas.expression: Non-modular: depends on BOTH levels. Semi-modular: only the DISTRIBUTARY level. Modular: NEITHER.
formulas.note: Semi-modules (open flume, orifice semi-module) dominate in practice; Gibb's module is the modular example.

formulas.label: Canal escape capacity
formulas.expression: about half the canal's full supply discharge
formulas.note: Escapes exist to prevent BREACHING, not for convenience. Scouring escapes have their sill at bed level.
